meeting.who: The Bank of England (“the BoE”), the UK’s central bank. Its interest rate is set by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): nine people, led by Governor Andrew Bailey. Five work at the Bank and four are “external” experts from outside. Each member votes, and the Bank publishes every vote by name, so we can see exactly who wanted what.

verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep Bank Rate where it is, at 3.75%. This remains an extremely tight call as inflation climbs to 3.5% and services prices accelerate.
verdict.confidence_note: “Low” means this is close to a coin flip. With inflation hitting 3.5% and services inflation moving up to 3.7%, the pressure on the MPC to act is intense.
verdict.short_version: UK prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August, with core inflation at 2.8% and services inflation at 3.7%. The BoE expects inflation to go above 4% early next year due to energy bills. Three members already voted for a rise in September, and these fresh inflation numbers bring a rate increase into very sharp focus. We think a narrow hold is still fractionally more likely as the committee waits for the full November forecast, but a raise is now nearly a coin flip.
verdict.card_why: CPI inflation jumped to 3.5% in September and services inflation ticked up to 3.7%, keeping a November rate rise on a knife-edge.
verdict.last_move: Cut 0.25 pts on Dec 18, 2025; held since (6–3 on Sep 17, 2026)

why_steps.title: The BoE has one main job, and one main tool
why_steps.html: By law, the Bank of England’s main job is to keep prices steady. The government sets its target: prices should rise about 2% a year, measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI, from the Office for National Statistics, the ONS). If inflation moves more than 1 percentage point away from 2%, the Governor must write a public open letter to the Chancellor explaining why and what the Bank will do. He had to write one in September (BoE). Its main tool is Bank Rate, the interest rate the BoE pays banks on money they keep with it. It flows through to tracker mortgages, savings accounts and business loans. Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting the rate is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is. Today Bank Rate is 3.75%, where it has been since December 2025 (BoE).

why_steps.title: Prices are rising faster, led by energy and services
why_steps.html: Consumer prices were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, up from 3.1% in August (ONS). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost £100 a year ago now costs about £103.50. The goal would be £102. The main driver remains energy costs. Motor fuel prices are up 29.8% in a year. Underneath, core prices (leaving out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, and prices of services such as haircuts, rents and restaurants ticked up to 3.7% from 3.4%. The BoE’s staff expect inflation to reach about 3¾% by the end of 2026 and slightly above 4% in early 2027, as household energy bills rise and firms pass on higher costs (BoE).

why_steps.title: The real question: are energy costs spreading?
why_steps.html: The BoE cannot make oil cheaper. What it can do is stop a one-off jump in fuel turning into a lasting habit of rising prices. Economists call that spreading “second-round effects”: workers ask for bigger pay rises to cover their bills, firms raise prices to cover their wage and energy costs, and people start to expect high inflation as normal. Evidence from the latest ONS releases shows both core CPI and services inflation ticking up. Firms in the BoE’s monthly business survey expect their prices to rise over the coming year, and wage growth expectations remain steady at 3.4% (DMP). Governor Bailey noted that while feed-through has been subdued so far, it is early days.

why_steps.title: Reasons the BoE might wait in November
why_steps.html:
• The majority set a clear test. In September six of nine members voted to hold. Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli noted that a majority of the MPC have not judged that an increase in Bank Rate is needed (speech).
  • Pay growth remains moderate overall. Although regular pay ticked up to 3.7% in August, forward-looking surveys indicate wage pressures are contained.
  • Job vacancies are cooling. Vacancies fell to 691,000 in September, showing some softening in employer demand (ONS).
  • Markets already pressed the brake. The 10-year gilt yield is 5.31%. Fixed mortgages follow these market rates, and lenders already reported a sharp fall in demand for home loans (BoE survey).
  • The Budget comes first. The government presents its Budget (OBR). Tax and spending changes could alter the inflation picture.

why_steps.title: Reasons the BoE might raise in November
why_steps.html:
• Inflation is heading above 4% and September CPI printed higher at 3.5%, with services up to 3.7%.
  • The swing voters are leaning toward a rise. Lombardelli stated that policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist (speech).
  • The Governor’s latest words were firm. On October 8, Bailey said interest rates may need to rise even as economic activity weakens (speech).
  • November is a forecast meeting. The BoE publishes a full new forecast with its decision, making it an ideal time to shift policy.
  • Three members already voted to raise in September (Greene, Mann, and Pill).

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

left: Lombardelli and Bailey hint a rise may be needed
right: Regular pay growth at 3.7% with cooling vacancies
Unemployment at 4.7% but job market mixed
Gilt rates already up; mortgage demand down
Majority previously sought clearer signs of spreading

why_steps.html: Both sides are exceptionally strong following the higher September inflation print. What tips us very slightly toward Hold is that the majority previously emphasized waiting for definitive evidence of second-round wage-price spirals, and the recent Budget introduces fiscal uncertainties. What pushes Raise so close is that CPI reached 3.5% and services inflation accelerated to 3.7%, fulfilling the risk conditions highlighted by hawkish members. That is why our probabilities stand at 50% Hold, 47% Raise and 3% Cut.

timeline.title: Holding at 4%, with the committee split
timeline.what: The MPC kept Bank Rate at 4% both times. In September the vote was 7–2. In November it was 5–4. In September the BoE also agreed to shrink its holdings of government bonds by £70 billion over the following year.
timeline.why: Inflation was high (3.8% in August 2025) but the BoE judged it had peaked.
timeline.people: Mortgage and savings rates stayed roughly the same.
timeline.because: one more soft inflation reading was enough to tip the balance.

timeline.title: A cut to 3.75%, by a single vote
timeline.what: The MPC lowered Bank Rate from 4% to 3.75%, by 5 votes to 4. Governor Bailey joined the four who had wanted a cut. The BoE said rates were likely to follow a gradual downward path.
timeline.why: Inflation had fallen to 3.2% in November, and the economy and job market looked soft.
timeline.people: Tracker and variable-rate mortgages got a little cheaper.

timeline.title: A pause, but still talking about cuts
timeline.what: Bank Rate stayed at 3.75%, by 5 votes to 4. The BoE said Bank Rate was likely to be reduced further.
timeline.why: Inflation was 3.4% in December, but the BoE expected it to fall toward 2% from April.
timeline.people: Borrowers were told cheaper loans were coming.
timeline.because: the BoE was preparing to cut when energy prices started soaring.

timeline.title: An energy shock: all nine vote to hold
timeline.what: All nine members voted to hold at 3.75%. The BoE noted that conflict in the Middle East caused a significant increase in global energy and commodity prices.
timeline.why: With energy prices jumping, cutting rates would have added fuel to inflation.
timeline.people: Petrol, diesel and household bills went up.
timeline.because: the debate flipped from when to cut to whether to raise.

timeline.title: The first votes for a rise
timeline.what: In April the vote was 8–1 to hold, with Huw Pill voting to raise. In June it was 7–2 as Megan Greene joined him.
timeline.why: Uncertainty over global energy prices prompted fears that waiting would let higher inflation take root.
timeline.people: Inflation eased temporarily, giving families relief.
timeline.because: each meeting added another member to the raise side.

timeline.title: Three votes to raise; oil had eased
timeline.what: The MPC held by 6 votes to 3; Catherine Mann joined Greene and Pill in wanting 4%. Inflation had dipped to 2.6% in June.
timeline.why: With oil temporarily lower, most members saw no immediate need to act.
timeline.people: The household energy price cap rose to £1,663 for July–September.

timeline.title: Held at 3.75% by 6–3, with an open letter
timeline.what: Same vote as July: Greene, Mann and Pill wanted 4%. Staff expected inflation of about 3¾% by year-end and slightly above 4% in early 2027. The Governor wrote an open letter to the Chancellor.
timeline.people: The energy price cap for October–December is set at £1,723.
timeline.because: inflation exceeded target by over 1 point, triggering an open letter.

timeline.title: Oil shifts, gilt rates climb, the pound slips
timeline.what: Brent oil reached $123.10 a barrel and WTI reached $103.37 a barrel. The 10-year gilt rate is 5.31%; the 5-year is 4.96%. One pound is US$1.3375 and €1.1979.
timeline.why: Higher oil means higher expected inflation, pushing investors to demand higher yields.
timeline.people: Fixed-rate mortgage deals are priced off these market rates, pushing new fixes higher.
timeline.because: market conditions tightened as energy price pressures persisted.

timeline.title: September CPI jumps to 3.5%
timeline.what: The ONS reported that headline CPI inflation rose to 3.5% in September, with core CPI at 2.8% and services inflation ticking up to 3.7%.
timeline.why: Shows energy shocks continuing to ripple through the broader economy, bringing a November rate rise into intense focus.
timeline.people: Households face sustained pressure on living costs.
timeline.because: our reading is that a rate rise is now on a knife-edge ahead of November 5.

choices.title: Hold: keep Bank Rate at 3.75%
choices.meaning: the BoE keeps its foot where it is while studying the new November macroeconomic forecast and upcoming Budget.
for: Pay and jobs remain mixed. Regular pay growth is 3.7% with cooling vacancies and unemployment at 4.7%.
Markets already tightened. The 10-year gilt rate is 5.31%, keeping borrowing conditions restrictive.
The Budget is imminent. Fiscal measures could alter the inflation outlook.
The majority’s caution. Previous statements emphasized waiting for conclusive signs of widespread second-round pressures.
against: CPI jumped to 3.5% and services to 3.7%. Inflation is well above target and accelerating.
Oil prices remain very high ($123.10 a barrel for Brent).
Three members already voted to raise in September.
Firm words from Governor Bailey on the necessity of acting even when activity slows.
choices.everyday: tracker mortgages and easy-access savings rates would stay roughly where they are. Markets would focus intensely on the December meeting.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 4.00%
choices.meaning: the BoE presses the brake to demonstrate resolve against persistent energy shocks and rising services inflation.
for: Inflation printed higher. September CPI rose to 3.5% and services inflation ticked up to 3.7%.
The condition is met. High energy prices have persisted, matching Lombardelli’s criteria for tightening.
Risk management. Hawkish members argue acting now prevents inflation expectations from unmooring.
A forecast meeting. November brings a full Monetary Policy Report to explain policy shifts.
against: Unemployment is at 4.7% with mixed wage signals.
Some members view spare capacity as sufficient to absorb shocks without a rate hike.
Financial markets have already done heavy lifting via higher gilt yields.
choices.everyday: tracker and variable mortgage payments would rise by roughly £21 a month per £100,000 of borrowing. Savings accounts would pay slightly more.

choices.title: Cut: lower Bank Rate
choices.meaning: the BoE pivots to support growth in the face of unexpected economic distress.
for: Only if a severe economic shock or financial crash occurred before November 5.
against: Inflation is 3.5% and rising. Cutting would add fuel.
Nobody voted for a cut since February 2026.
The active debate is entirely about holding or raising.
choices.everyday: loans would get slightly cheaper, but such a move would imply unexpected economic trouble.

change.lead: Our 50% / 47% / 3% guess is based on what we know today. New information arrives almost every day. Here is what we are watching, and why each item matters.
change.intro: The BoE can only react to information it has already seen. A report released before November 5 can change the November decision. A report released after it can only shape what happens on December 17.

retail_sales.why: Shows whether high fuel and energy costs are squeezing household spending.
retail_sales.trigger: A big drop leans Hold; a strong gain leans Raise.

budget_obr_economic_and_fiscal.why: The Budget will outline tax and spending plans alongside OBR forecasts.
budget_obr_economic_and_fiscal.trigger: Measures that materially cut inflation favor Hold; a loose fiscal stance pushing up gilt yields favors Raise.

gdp_first_estimate.why: Too late for November, but key for December.

uk_labour_market_2.why: Will show whether the job market keeps loosening.

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil, gas and the Middle East. Brent crude at $123.10 a barrel continues to drive inflation pressures.
Gilt rates and the pound. 10-year gilt yields at 5.31% reflect tight financial conditions.
Final words from MPC members. Speeches before November 5 provide the final policy hints.

report_card.one: CPI inflation rose to 3.5% in September, with services inflation at 3.7% and core at 2.8%.
report_card.look: Consumer prices (CPI, up 3.5%), CPIH (up 3.6%), core CPI (2.8%), services (3.7%), and factory input prices.
report_card.why: Inflation is well above target following energy shocks, and September figures showed acceleration in both core and services categories.
report_card.change: Oil and gas prices falling back decisively alongside a drop in services inflation.
report_card.matters: This is the core reason a rate rise is actively on the table.

report_card.one: Unemployment is at 4.7% and regular pay growth ticked up to 3.7%, while vacancies cooled to 691,000.
report_card.look: The unemployment rate, payroll jobs, job vacancies, and regular pay growth.
report_card.why: Unemployment ticked down to 4.7% for August and pay growth edged up to 3.7%, showing ongoing resilience alongside cooling vacancies.
report_card.change: Unemployment rising above 5% with falling pay growth → red.
report_card.matters: A balanced job market helps policymakers gauge second-round wage pressures.

report_card.one: The economy is growing modestly, but households remain cautious with a saving ratio of 8.8%.
report_card.look: GDP growth, monthly GDP, retail sales, and household saving.
report_card.why: Monthly GDP grew +0.1% in August and retail sales remain solid, but consumer caution persists.
report_card.change: Weak GDP figures and falling retail sales → red.
report_card.matters: Moderate growth gives the BoE room to wait, but does not rule out action against inflation.

report_card.one: Government borrowing costs remain elevated with 10-year gilt yields at 5.31%.
report_card.look: Gilt yields, SONIA, sterling exchange rates, and lending conditions.
report_card.why: 10-year gilt yields at 5.31% and 5-year yields at 4.96% keep borrowing conditions tight.
report_card.change: Gilt yields settling back toward 5% → yellow.
report_card.matters: Higher market rates slow the economy, doing some of the BoE's tightening work.

w: What it said: Bailey, Breeden, Dhingra, Lombardelli, Ramsden and Taylor voted to hold. Greene, Mann and Pill voted to raise to 4%. The Committee noted risks to inflation are tilted to the upside.
Why it matters: only two more votes are needed for a rate rise.

said.v: Assessing labor market slack and wage pressures
w: What it said: Greene examined whether labor market slack is sufficient to mitigate the latest supply shock and restrain wage-setting second-round effects.
Why it matters: highlights her ongoing hawkish stance against lingering inflation.

said.v: Leaning toward tightening if energy prices persist
w: What she said: policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.
Why it matters: as Deputy Governor, her potential switch is critical for the November outcome.
What he said: interest rates may need to rise even as economic activity weakens.
Why it matters: the Governor's tone remains a vital signal of majority sentiment.

said.pv: Voted to raise in July and September
w: What she said: our current monetary policy stance is not sufficiently tight, and she cannot take comfort from tighter financial market conditions.
Why it matters: she will continue voting to raise.

said.v: CPI expected about 3¾% in late 2026, slightly above 4% in early 2027
w: What it said: inflation of 3.1% in August was 1.1 points above target due largely to energy.
Why it matters: established the official expectation of higher inflation ahead.

group_intros.prices: These numbers show how fast prices are rising. The BoE’s target is 2% a year for CPI. With September CPI at 3.5% and services inflation at 3.7%, the BoE watches closely for second-round effects.
group_intros.jobs: These numbers track employment, vacancies, and pay growth. Fast pay growth can keep services inflation elevated.
group_intros.growth: These numbers show economic output and consumer spending. Moderate growth gives the BoE flexibility.
group_intros.rates: These numbers cover Bank Rate, market gilt yields, and overnight rates set by financial markets.

group_intros.global: The UK imports energy and trades extensively, making international commodity prices vital.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the BoE has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Note: FRED does not carry an up-to-date UK consumer price series (its OECD copy stops in March 2025), so for prices use the ONS directly. FRED’s UK 10-year gilt rate is a monthly average and its unemployment and GDP copies arrive months late, so they may differ from the daily and latest figures on this page.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website, or on the Bank of England’s own statistics database.
